newsitem.title: GERMANY: German parties square off ahead of tax talks.
newsitem.headline: German parties square off ahead of tax talks.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) were preparing compromise proposals on Friday for a weekend summit on tax reform, the issue seen as key to getting the German economy back on track.

Following two unsuccessful rounds of talks last week, the government is ready to give ground on Saturday on proposals to tax unemployment benefits and pensions if it can raise gasoline and value-added taxes by about 25 to 30 billion marks ($14.6 to $17.5 billion) instead, the Berliner Zeitung reported.
Government officials, commenting on the newspaper report, said no firm decisions had been made. In the past, SPD officials said they opposed a rise in VAT to finance tax reform.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel says his reform package, including a net 30 billion marks in tax cuts, will stimulate investment and create jobs. Weakness of the economy has caused concern about Germany's ability to meet targets to qualify for European economic and monetary union.
The SPD aims to steal Waigel's thunder by pressing him to implement the package next year, instead of in 1999. It also claims Waigel's planned tax cuts are not solidly offset by revenue measures.

"A compromise is possible and urgently needed. But some SPD demands, such as those about the top tax rate and taxation of night shifts, are not practical or would not serve to fight unemployment," said CDU vice chairman Christoph Bergner in an interview with the Magddeburger Zeitung.
Government officials say Saturday's talks will be decisive if a compromise is to be reached by Easter.
Waigel has said tax reform will proceed with or without the SPD. But the opposition could use its majority in the upper house of parliament to give any legislation a rough ride.
The atmosphere was polarised on Thursday as new data showed unemployment reached another postwar record in February. SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said this was a black mark on Kohl's government.
"The further increase in unemployment shows that the policies of the Kohl government have failed. Germany needs new economic and finance policies," Lafontaine said.
"As an immediate measure the SPD demands a reduction in social security charges and tax cuts for workers and families," he added.
A government plan for deep cuts in subsidies to the coal-mining industry will also cast a shadow on the tax talks.

The coalition, under pressure to rein in the deficit to qualify for a single European currency, proposed on Thursday to slash coal subsidies to 3.8 billion marks starting in 2005 from about 10 billion now.
The cuts would hit hardest in the coal-mining states of Saarland and North Rhine-Westphalia, which have SPD governments. SPD state officials have termed the plan a catastrophe.
The Berliner Zeitung also reported that the government was ready to accept a top tax rate a little above 40 percent, bowing to SPD opposition to a deeper cut. The top rate is now 53 percent.
The top tax rate, and government proposals to tax income from night- and holiday-shifts, were among the major stumbling blocks in earlier talks.
German industry groups have proposed that employers pay a 10 percent tax on workers' income from unsociable hours.

CDU officials were meeting on Friday morning to discuss the pension system, where they hoped reallocation of funds would free up about 15 billion marks. A refinancing of unemployment benefits is also under consideration.
